summary: Updates the VeriSign Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP) from the Network Solutions version 1.1.0 described in RFC 2832 to version 2.0.0. It describes the changes to apply on top of that base specification. RRP is how registrars interact with the registry for domain names. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you buy a web name, a shop tells the big name keeper about it. This document updates the rule book those shops use for talking to that keeper.

questions: what is the registry registrar protocol
how do registrars talk to registries
how to cancel a domain transfer
subtitle: Updates to the protocol registrars use to manage domain names with a registry.

tldr.problem: The RRP protocol (RFC 2832) lacked support for IPv6 and had incomplete handling of transfer cancellations, and domains with non-ASCII names needed better encoding validation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3632 adds two new response codes (510 for invalid encoding, 557 for locked nameservers), allows registrars to cancel pending transfer requests, and introduces support for IPv6 name server addresses.
tldr.outcome: These updates bring RRP to version 2.0.0, enabling registrars to manage internationalized domains and giving them finer control over transfer requests while supporting the growing IPv6 Internet.

today: RFC 2832 (RRP v1.1.0) is updated to version 2.0.0 by RFC 3632, which remains an Informational document. Together they specify the protocol registrars use to manage domain registrations in registries.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RRP (Registry Registrar Protocol) is how domain registrars communicate with the registry that manages a top-level domain (TLD). RFC 3632 updates version 1.1.0, originally published as RFC 2832, to version 2.0.0 and adds capabilities that were missing.

The update enables internationalized domain name validation, gives registrars control over pending transfers, and adds IPv6 support to address evolving needs in the DNS ecosystem.
sections.eli5: RRP is the rule book shops use when talking to the name database about web names they are managing for customers. This update adds three new rules to that book.

sections.title: Response Codes and Validation
sections.content:
RFC 3632 introduces two new response codes. 510 (Invalid encoding) tells a registrar that a domain name or nameserver name contains invalid ASCII compatible encoding (the standard way to represent non-ASCII domain and host names). This error is checked when adding an internationalized domain or nameserver, or when changing a nameserver name to an internationalized one.

557 (Name server locked) indicates that a nameserver is hosting a TLD in the root zone of DNS and cannot be modified or deleted without approval from IANA and the U.S. Department of Commerce. This protection ensures root infrastructure stability.
sections.eli5: Two new error messages tell the shop: "that name is written wrong" and "that server can't be changed without permission from the very top people."

sections.title: Transfer Request Cancellation
sections.content:
Under RFC 2832, once a registrar requested a domain transfer, the request could only be approved or rejected by the sponsoring registrar or implicitly approved after a fixed time. RFC 3632 adds a new capability: the requesting registrar may now cancel a pending transfer request using an updated TRANSFER command with -Approve:No.

The cancellation must be sent before the sponsoring registrar explicitly approves or rejects the request, or before the registry implicitly approves or rejects it. This gives registrars more operational flexibility.
sections.eli5: If you ask to move a web name to a different shop, you can now say "never mind" before anyone says yes or no.

sections.title: IPv6 Name Server Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 2832 was written before IPv6 became common. RFC 3632 adds grammar to the RRP protocol to support IPv6 address notation alongside the existing IPv4 support.

The RFC includes ABNF (Augmented Backus-Naur Form) grammar for both standard IPv6 notation (eight groups of 1 to 4 hex digits separated by colons, such as 10AA:0:0:00:8:800:200C:417A) and compressed notation (using :: to represent runs of zeros). This lets registrars specify nameservers using modern addressing.
sections.eli5: The update teaches the system how to write down IPv6 addresses (the newer, longer type of internet address) so nameservers can use them.
